turns.speaker: Guest Speaker 1
turns.text: My name is Reese Lindmark, and you're listening to Gray Mirror, a podcast from MIT Media Lab's Digital Currency Initiative on technology, society, and ethics. And unlike something like Black Mirror, which just looks at the negative impacts of technology on society, we are Gray Mirror, so we look at the positive and negative impacts of technology on society. And please, if you have any feedback, reach out on Twitter, and if you like the show, give us a five-star rating on your favorite podcast app. We really do appreciate it. Thanks.

turns.speaker: Guest Speaker 1
turns.text: everybody. So today I interview Kelsey Piper, who's a journalist at Future Perfect, which is this effective altruist-inspired publication from Vox. And we have a... wide-ranging discussion as one does on podcasts, you know, about a variety of different things, what it's like to write about effective altruist stuff for a general audience, which, by the way, as a side of here, it's just so cool that there's now a real thing, i.e. Vox, that talks about effective altruist stuff and is effective altruist inspired. I think that's good for society. I'm not saying all effective... All media outlets should be effective altruist inspired, but just have a couple. Feels fine. So we chat about that. We chat about her article about, you know, climate change and why it's not an actual existential risk, but it's obviously a big risk, but why that differentiation is important. We chat about the norms around the safe release of GPT2, which is an AI language generating software. But I want to kind of highlight two big... points here. The first is we chat about social justice activism versus effective altruism as mindsets and why they are sometimes compatible, sometimes not compatible. I think Kelsey makes two pretty cool points about this. The first is that with social justice activism, they're very suspicious of people speaking on others' behalf. And they put a lot of weight. Socialist activists put a lot of weight on people's lived experience. And that's all reasonable and very powerful. It's like speaking if someone else is like, it's like a neocolonialist vibe where you're like, oh, I think that I know it's best for these people, therefore I speak for them. And that's generally good to be wary of those things. But for things like animals or for future people who can't speak for themselves,

turns.speaker: Guest Speaker 1
turns.text: then how should that be part of the social justice activist lens or the mindset there? And then the other piece here is, you know, the social justice activist perspective on systems of oppression and power, which again is a very powerful perspective. It's kind of a justice-oriented perspective where you say, oh, boy, there are these, like, bad people in power, and they're doing these bad things, and they're being oppressive or they're using their power in bad ways, and we want justice. And so this has worked for a while in terms of pushing back on past problems like slavery or the, you know, prison pipeline or whatever. But... It's difficult to have that similar perspective with things like AI safety or other existential kind of exponential risks where there's no real bad actor. There's no real injustice that's happening. It's just kind of it's mollick, right? It's incentives gone wrong with just well-intentioned people trying to do their... their best and even if everybody's well-intentioned and thinking from a good, you know, justice framework, it still might not work and, you know, many people may die from some of these things. So, yeah, this is to say that social justice activism, it's really good at looking at the system and how power and oppression work within the system, but it's probably less good when looking at how incentives or technology work within the system. So this is to say that whenever you're putting on a hat or lens or a perspective, whether it's effective altruist or social justice activism, think about what problems does it make legible? Which ones can it see? And then which ones is it not as good at tackling or which ones are, is it less good at exploring? So that's the first big point here. And then the second big point is... around what Kelsey calls

turns.speaker: Guest Speaker 1
turns.text: world. And so that's this idea of cultural revolution. And you can pretty much see that here with tech where it's like when this new tech thing pops up.

turns.speaker: Guest Speaker 1
turns.text: addition to maybe responding with code or with laws or whatever, you can also respond from this cultural evolution or memetic immunity perspective where you say, hey, these things might be initially hurtful to society and humanity, but we're going to kind of as a population be... be able to reject them or get immunity to them or evolve new cultural norms around them that are more beneficial for us and society. So enjoy today's episode. Goodbye.
